content_of_post_to_comment:
Habits I frame as "add this good thing to your day" tend to die in about two weeks. Walking was one of them for years.

What changed it was a shift in framing I stumbled into. For nearly all of human history, sitting still all day literally wasn't possible — the whole day was reasons to be on your feet. Constant walking was the background condition everything else in the body got built on. The all-day-sedentary life is the genuinely new thing, historically speaking.

So I stopped treating walking as a virtuous add-on I had to motivate myself into, and started treating sitting all day as the deviation. Subtle, but it killed the guilt-and-willpower framing that always burned me out. I'm not forcing a new habit uphill; I'm just returning to a default when I've drifted too far from it. And the bar is low — the mood/focus payoff shows up after ~10 minutes, so there's no "wasn't long enough to count."

Been the most durable version of the habit I've had. Sharing in case the reframe helps someone else who keeps falling off.
comment: The shift from 'I need to add exercise' to 'I need to undo a modern habit' is a pretty powerful distinction. I've noticed the same with sleep routines too — trying to optimize everything creates pressure, but removing the thing that’s throwing you off often feels easier. Makes me wonder how many habits fail because we frame normal maintenance as a self-improvement project.
